claim: Böcklin (born Basel, 16 October 1827) was a Swiss painter working in Florence in 1880, aged 52; known for mythological scenes (gods, sea creatures, nymphs) and famous in Germany
In spring (April) 1880 the young widow Marie Berna visited Böcklin's studio in Florence, where the first version stood unfinished, and asked for 'ein Bild zum Träumen' (a picture to dream by)
Marie Berna was born Marie Christ in New York (1846); she married Georg Berna in 1864; Georg Berna died on 18 October 1865, of diphtheria, aged 29
She commissioned the picture in memory of her late husband
Böcklin painted her the second version (June 1880, oil on wood), now in the Metropolitan Museum
The coffin and the white-shrouded figure were added at Berna's request according to en.wikipedia (de.wikipedia: added soon after, to this and the first version) — narrated as 'many accounts say'

Böcklin's letter of 29 June 1880: the picture 'Die Gräberinsel' (Tomb Island) was sent off; 'Sie werden sich hineinträumen können in die Welt der Schatten … Bis sie Scheu haben werden die feierliche Stille durch ein lautes Wort zu stören' (paraphrased in the narration)
Marie Berna married Count Waldemar von Oriola on 18 December 1880 and owned the painting until her death in 1915; the Met acquired it in 1926
Self-Portrait with Death Playing the Fiddle, 1872, Alte Nationalgalerie: Death plays a fiddle behind the painter, who holds a brush
Böcklin and Angela Pascucci had fourteen children; he lost eight of them (five died in childhood, three more before him)
Daughter Maria Anna Böcklin died on 20 March 1877 aged 7 months and is buried in the English Cemetery, Florence, close to Böcklin's studio
The English Cemetery is a walled hill with cypresses; that it inspired the island is a hedged suggestion (de.wikipedia: 'denkbar', per Olaf Metzel)
Pontikonisi near Corfu is sometimes named as the model, but Böcklin never went there (unconfirmed)
Böcklin spent autumn 1879 on Ischia and saw the Castello Aragonese; the museum says the motif may have come back to him when Berna asked (hedged)
The third version (1883, oil on wood, 80 × 150 cm) was commissioned by the Berlin dealer Fritz Gurlitt
The title 'Die Toteninsel' comes not from Böcklin but from his dealer Fritz Gurlitt
From the third version on, one of the burial chambers in the rocks on the right bears Böcklin's initials 'A.B.'
Gurlitt had Max Klinger make an etching of the painting (1890)
The Berlin museum: it was this version that founded the picture's extraordinary fame ('die den außerordentlichen Ruhm des Bildes … begründete')
Fourth version 1884; fifth version 1886, commissioned for the Leipzig museum (Museum der bildenden Künste)
Böcklin died on 16 January 1901 near Florence (San Domenico, Fiesole) and was buried in Florence (Cimitero degli Allori)
A 1901 version signed 'A. Böcklin invenit' / 'Carlo Böcklin fecit 1901' by his son Carlo after his design; now in the Hermitage
Reproductions were hugely popular in Germany; Nabokov's novel Despair (1936) says prints could be found in every Berlin home
Strindberg's The Ghost Sonata (1907) ends with Böcklin's Island of the Dead seen in the distance
Rachmaninoff, then living in Dresden, saw a black-and-white reproduction in Paris in May 1907
He composed the symphonic poem Isle of the Dead, Op. 29, in 1909 and conducted its premiere in Moscow
The recurring 5/8 figure may depict the oarsman's rowing or the movement of the water
He was disappointed by the colour original: 'If I had seen first the original, I, probably, would have not written my Isle of the Dead. I like it in black and white.' (as quoted)
The painting inspired nearly thirty compositions (FAZ); Max Reger's 'Die Toteninsel' is No. 3 of his Böcklin suite, Op. 128 (1913)
De Chirico: 'Each of Böcklin's works is a shock'; Surrealists such as Max Ernst and Salvador Dalí admired Böcklin
Dalí, 1932: 'Le Vrai Tableau de « L'Île des morts » d'Arnold Böcklin à l'heure de l'Angélus', oil on canvas, Von der Heydt-Museum, Wuppertal
Dalí leaves the link between title and scene for the viewer to work out
The Angelus is the evening prayer; Dalí was obsessed with Millet's The Angelus
1934: Dalí's 'Cour centrale de l'Île des morts (obsession reconstitutive d'après Böcklin)' and 'Cour ouest de l'Île des morts (obsession reconstitutive d'après Böcklin)'
Hitler at one time owned 11 Böcklin paintings (NYT, 12 Jan 2002, via en.wikipedia)

Provenance: Gurlitt 1884 → Schön, Worms → Zürich/Rheineck → St. Gallen → Chemnitz → Munich → Sturzenegger, St. Gallen 1931–36 → Munich dealers (Fritz Nathan; Maria Almas-Dietrich) 1936 → Verwaltung der Reichskanzlei, Berlin, 1936–1945 → missing → bought 1980 from Wolfgang Böttger, former consul general
It hung at the Berghof and from 1940 in the New Reich Chancellery (Birgit Schwarz, Geniewahn, 2009)
The fourth version, later in Heinrich Thyssen's Berlin bank branch, burned in a WWII bombing raid; only a black-and-white photograph survives
Today: second version Met, New York; first version Kunstmuseum Basel (Böcklin's home town); fifth version Leipzig
Spring 2027 (19 March – 1 August), for Böcklin's 200th birthday, the Alte Nationalgalerie reunites all four surviving versions for the first time; 'Selbst Böcklin sah die Werke nie versammelt'
